name: Memory Safety & Exploitation
description: Memory-corruption bugs, exploitation techniques, and mitigations (ASLR, CFI, sanitizers).

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers here, all from USENIX 2018, frame memory safety as a two-sided arms race. On the offensive side, the community pushed hard on automation: FUZE (USENIX 2018) tackled facilitating exploit generation for kernel use-after-free bugs, while HeapHopper (USENIX 2018) brought bounded model checking to heap allocator security and Automatic Heap Layout Manipulation for Exploitation (USENIX 2018) automated the heap grooming that real exploits depend on. On the defensive side, the same year emphasized shrinking and isolating the attack surface, with Debloating Software through Piece-Wise Compilation and Loading (USENIX 2018) removing unused code and IMIX: In-Process Memory Isolation EXtension (USENIX 2018) carving out protected regions inside a process. The Guard's Dilemma (USENIX 2018) showed that even Intel SGX enclaves were not immune to efficient code-reuse attacks.

A clear shift followed in 2019-2020 toward hardware-assisted, fine-grained isolation and toward stress-testing control-flow defenses. ERIM (USENIX 2019) made in-process isolation with Intel MPK protection keys practical and efficient, and Donky (USENIX 2020) extended that protection-key model to RISC-V and x86. At the same time, defenders refined control-flow integrity with Origin-sensitive Control Flow Integrity (USENIX 2019), while CONFIRM (USENIX 2019) delivered a sobering evaluation of how compatible and relevant existing CFI protections actually were for modern software. Exploit automation kept pace through KEPLER (USENIX 2019) and KOOBE (USENIX 2020), which targeted control-flow hijacking primitives and kernel out-of-bounds writes. Crucially, this period exposed that the new isolation primitives were themselves attackable: PKU Pitfalls (USENIX 2020) demonstrated attacks on PKU-based memory isolation, foreshadowing a recurring theme.

By 2021-2022 the field had matured into a back-and-forth over both software defenses and the hardware substrate. Defensive allocator design advanced with Preventing Use-After-Free Attacks with Fast Forward Allocation (USENIX 2021), and kernel attack surface reduction continued with SHARD (USENIX 2021). But a parallel front opened around physical-layer DRAM attacks: SMASH (USENIX 2021) revived Rowhammer from JavaScript despite in-DRAM TRR mitigations, Half-Double (USENIX 2022) extended hammering to non-adjacent rows, and RETBLEED (USENIX 2022) showed arbitrary speculative code execution via return instructions. The isolation-attack theme also recurred, with Jenny (USENIX 2022) securing syscalls for PKU-based systems after earlier attacks. Most recently, ZenHammer (USENIX 2024) carried Rowhammer onto AMD Zen platforms, confirming that even as software mitigations harden, hardware-level memory corruption remains an open and evolving threat.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this list, from NDSS 2018, already shows the two poles that would define the field: finding memory-corruption bugs and stopping their exploitation. On the discovery side, "IoTFuzzer: Discovering Memory Corruptions in IoT Through App-based Fuzzing" (NDSS 2018) and "What You Corrupt Is Not What You Crash: Challenges in Fuzzing Embedded Devices" (NDSS 2018) pushed fuzzing into hard-to-instrument embedded targets, while "K-Miner: Uncovering Memory Corruption in Linux" (NDSS 2018) applied static analysis to the kernel. On the defense side, "CFIXX: Object Type Integrity for C++" (NDSS 2018) and "Back To The Epilogue: Evading Control Flow Guard via Unaligned Targets" (NDSS 2018) framed the cat-and-mouse of control-flow integrity (CFI) that runs through the whole decade.

The next few years split into sharper specializations. Use-after-free became its own thread, starting with "CRCount: Pointer Invalidation with Reference Counting to Mitigate Use-after-free in Legacy C/C++" (NDSS 2019). Embedded and data-only threats grew up: "µRAI: Securing Embedded Systems with Return Address Integrity" (NDSS 2020) hardened backward edges on microcontrollers, and "NoJITsu: Locking Down JavaScript Engines" (NDSS 2020) confronted data-only attacks in scripting runtimes. CFI kept maturing with binary-level work like "Refining Indirect Call Targets at the Binary Level" (NDSS 2021) and the measurement lens of "CFInsight: A Comprehensive Metric for CFI Policies" (NDSS 2022). Meanwhile defenses moved toward isolation and compartmentalization — "Preventing Kernel Hacks with HAKCs" (NDSS 2022) and "The Taming of the Stack: Isolating Stack Data from Memory Errors" (NDSS 2022) — and "Cross-Language Attacks" (NDSS 2022) warned that mixing safe and unsafe languages opens new corruption paths.

By the mid-2020s the field broadened from software-only bugs into hardware-level and offense-oriented territory. Rowhammer defenses like "Copy-on-Flip: Hardening ECC Memory Against Rowhammer Attacks" (NDSS 2023) sat alongside exploitation aids such as "Towards Automatic and Precise Heap Layout Manipulation for General-Purpose Programs" (NDSS 2023) and backward-edge bypasses in "Let Me Unwind That For You: Exceptions to Backward-Edge Protection" (NDSS 2023). Kernel exploitation and assessment matured with "K-LEAK: Towards Automating the Generation of Multi-Step Infoleak Exploits against the Linux Kernel" (NDSS 2024) and "SyzBridge" (NDSS 2024). In 2025, classic mitigations got revisited under new pressure — "Oreo: Protecting ASLR Against Microarchitectural Attacks" (NDSS 2025) and "type++: Prohibiting Type Confusion with Inline Type Information" (NDSS 2025) — while "Wallbleed: A Memory Disclosure Vulnerability in the Great Firewall of China" (NDSS 2025) showed a real-world buffer over-read at internet scale.

The most recent NDSS 2026 papers make clear the frontier is now equal parts hardware, kernel, and automation. Rowhammer remains unresolved and empirical, with "Memory Band-Aid: A Principled Rowhammer Defense-in-Depth" (NDSS 2026) and the large-scale prevalence study "FLIPPYRAM" (NDSS 2026). Kernel offense keeps advancing through "PhantomMap: GPU-Assisted Kernel Exploitation" (NDSS 2026), "DirtyFree: Simplified Data-Oriented Programming in the Linux Kernel" (NDSS 2026), and "Cross-Cache Attacks for the Linux Kernel via PCP Massaging" (NDSS 2026), while the "SoK: Take a Deep Step into Linux Kernel Hardening Effectiveness" (NDSS 2026) steps back to weigh how much all these defenses actually buy. Long-standing bug classes still get fresh takes — "Fast Pointer Nullification for Use-After-Free Prevention" and "IsolatOS: Detecting Double Fetch Bugs in COTS RTOS" (both NDSS 2026) — and the field is beginning to fold in machine learning, as "What Do They Fix? LLM-Aided Categorization of Security Patches for Critical Memory Bugs" (NDSS 2026) uses large language models to triage the very bugs this area has spent a decade chasing.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice attacks the problem from two directions at once: the fragility of hardware and the fragility of control flow. On the hardware side, "Another Flip in the Wall of Rowhammer Defenses" (S&P 2018) showed that DRAM disturbance bugs could be triggered even against systems that thought they had closed the door, kicking off a long arms race. On the software side, "Compiler-Assisted Code Randomization" (S&P 2018) and "Protecting the Stack with Metadata Policies and Tagged Hardware" (S&P 2018) reflected the field's two dominant mitigation philosophies of the era — randomize the layout so attackers cannot find their gadgets, or tag data in hardware so corruption is caught structurally. "SoK: Shining Light on Shadow Stacks" (S&P 2019) took stock of how well control-flow defenses were actually holding up.

The next few years were defined by attacks that broke the assumptions those defenses rested on. "Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution" (S&P 2019) showed that the CPU's own performance machinery could leak secrets across every boundary, and "Exploiting Correcting Codes" (S&P 2019) demonstrated that even ECC memory did not stop Rowhammer. Meanwhile the community began treating memory safety as something to systematize and measure rather than merely propose: "SoK: Sanitizing for Security" (S&P 2019) mapped the sanitizer design space. A parallel thread pushed toward stronger foundations — CHERI's capability hardware, with "Cornucopia: Temporal Safety for CHERI Heaps" (S&P 2020) and "Rigorous engineering for hardware security" (S&P 2020) tackling use-after-free and formal assurance, while "MarkUs" (S&P 2020) offered a drop-in temporal-safety defense for ordinary C/C++.

By the early 2020s two trends dominate. Rowhammer keeps escalating — "BLACKSMITH" (S&P 2022) defeated in-DRAM mitigations with non-uniform patterns, prompting new defenses like "REGA" (S&P 2023). And the field pivoted hard toward compartmentalization: isolating buggy code so a corruption cannot spread, seen across "SEIMI" (S&P 2020), "μSwitch" (S&P 2023), "SecureCells" (S&P 2023), and several embedded-systems privilege-separation papers (S&P 2023). Attackers answered in kind — "WarpAttack" (S&P 2023) bypassed CFI through compiler-introduced double-fetches, and kernel-focused tools like "GREBE" (S&P 2022) and "AEM" (S&P 2023) made real-world exploitability, not just bug-finding, the object of study.

The most recent work shows the frontier moving onto commodity tagging hardware and back into the kernel, with the attackers keeping pace. "Sticky Tags" (S&P 2024) and "NanoTag" (S&P 2026) build efficient spatial-safety enforcement on ARM's memory tagging, even as "Tiktag" (S&P 2025) breaks that same tagging extension using speculative execution. Defenses like Intel CET are being chained around in "Crashing Through Defenses: Exploiting Segfaults and Chaining Around Intel CET" (S&P 2026), and kernel exploitation continues to advance in "HEAP LOCALIZATION" (S&P 2026) and "NetPanic" (S&P 2026). Rowhammer has jumped to new hardware in "GDDRHammer" (S&P 2026) and earned its own retrospective in "SoK: Systematizing a Decade of Architectural Rowhammer Defenses" (S&P 2026). Notably, the field is also turning its tools on itself and on new languages — "Evaluating the Effectiveness of Memory Safety Sanitizers" (S&P 2025) audits the defenses grad students rely on daily, and "deepSURF" (S&P 2026) uses LLM-augmented fuzzing to hunt memory-safety bugs in Rust, signaling that even memory-safe languages are now part of this story.

ccs.narrative:
Memory safety and exploitation research at CCS has tracked the ongoing arms race between mitigations and attacker innovations. The 2018 cohort examined CFI and its limits from both sides: Enforcing Unique Code Target Property for Control-Flow Integrity (CCS 2018) tightened CFI by mapping each call site to a unique target, while Block Oriented Programming: Automating Data-Only Attacks (CCS 2018) automated the construction of data-only payloads that bypass CFI entirely. Revery: From Proof-of-Concept to Exploitable (CCS 2018) bridged the crash-to-exploit gap automatically.

Kernel exploitation was examined through heap manipulation: SLAKE: Facilitating Slab Manipulation for Exploiting Vulnerabilities in the Linux Kernel (CCS 2019) automated Linux slab heap grooming to enable reliable kernel exploitation. The interaction between speculation and memory safety produced Speculative Probing: Hacking Blind in the Spectre Era (CCS 2020), showing that speculative execution eliminates the need for info-leak gadgets in ASLR bypass.

Rust's memory safety guarantees were scrutinized at both the language and enclave level: Towards Memory Safe Enclave Programming with Rust-SGX (CCS 2019) brought Rust's ownership model to SGX enclaves, while MirChecker: Detecting Bugs in Rust Programs via Static Analysis (CCS 2021) showed that unsafe blocks and integer overflows remain exploitable even in Rust. DirtyCred: Escalating Privilege in Linux Kernel (CCS 2022) bypassed SMEP, SMAP, and KASLR using kernel credential-object swapping.

milestones.title: Enforcing Unique Code Target Property for Control-Flow Integrity
milestones.note: Strengthened CFI to unique per-callsite targets, closing the over-approximation that coarse-grained CFI permits.

milestones.title: Block Oriented Programming: Automating Data-Only Attacks
milestones.note: Automated data-only exploit construction using block-oriented programming to bypass CFI mitigations.

milestones.title: Revery: From Proof-of-Concept to Exploitable
milestones.note: Automated the transformation of crash PoCs into working exploits by exploring exploitable program states.

milestones.title: SLAKE: Facilitating Slab Manipulation for Exploiting Vulnerabilities in the Linux Kernel
milestones.note: Automated Linux slab heap grooming to reliably exploit kernel heap vulnerabilities.

milestones.title: Towards Memory Safe Enclave Programming with Rust-SGX
milestones.note: Applied Rust's memory-safety guarantees to SGX enclave programming to prevent memory corruption inside enclaves.

milestones.title: Speculative Probing: Hacking Blind in the Spectre Era
milestones.note: Used speculative execution to defeat ASLR without any info-leak vulnerability, fundamentally changing ASLR assumptions.

milestones.title: MirChecker: Detecting Bugs in Rust Programs via Static Analysis
milestones.note: Found exploitable bugs in Rust's unsafe code via MIR-level static analysis, showing Rust is not unconditionally safe.

milestones.title: DirtyCred: Escalating Privilege in Linux Kernel
milestones.note: Bypassed all modern Linux kernel mitigations by swapping credential kernel objects during exploitation.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list, from 2018, is really two conversations happening at once. One is about finding memory-corruption bugs where they are hardest to reach: inside embedded and IoT firmware, as in "IoTFuzzer: Discovering Memory Corruptions in IoT Through App-based Fuzzing" (NDSS 2018) and "What You Corrupt Is Not What You Crash: Challenges in Fuzzing Embedded Devices" (NDSS 2018). The other is about turning a crash into a working exploit, which "FUZE: Towards Facilitating Exploit Generation for Kernel Use-After-Free Vulnerabilities" (USENIX 2018), "Revery: From Proof-of-Concept to Exploitable" (CCS 2018), and "HeapHopper: Bringing Bounded Model Checking to Heap Implementation Security" (USENIX 2018) each attacked from a different angle. Running underneath both was a defensive arms race: Control-Flow Integrity was being tightened in "Enforcing Unique Code Target Property for Control-Flow Integrity" (CCS 2018), even as "Block Oriented Programming: Automating Data-Only Attacks" (CCS 2018) showed that attackers could simply route around CFI with data-only attacks. Isolation and diversification appeared as complementary defenses in "Compiler-Assisted Code Randomization" (S&P 2018) and "IMIX: In-Process Memory Isolation EXtension" (USENIX 2018).

Around 2019 the field widened in two directions. First, exploitation research moved deeper into the Linux kernel, with "SLAKE: Facilitating Slab Manipulation for Exploiting Vulnerabilities in the Linux Kernel" (CCS 2019) and "KEPLER: Facilitating Control-flow Hijacking Primitive Evaluation for Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities" (USENIX 2019) formalizing the heap-grooming and primitive-chaining steps that had been folklore. Second, the community started taking stock: "SoK: Sanitizing for Security" (S&P 2019) and "SoK: Shining Light on Shadow Stacks" (S&P 2019) mapped out the detection and mitigation toolbox. Two developments reshaped the threat model entirely. "Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution" (S&P 2019) turned CPU speculation into a memory-disclosure channel, and the Rowhammer line matured from "Another Flip in the Wall of Rowhammer Defenses" (S&P 2018) through "Exploiting Correcting Codes: On the Effectiveness of ECC Memory Against Rowhammer Attacks" (S&P 2019) and "SPOILER" (USENIX 2019), demonstrating that even ECC and speculative-load behavior gave attackers new leverage.

Into 2020-2022 the center of gravity shifted toward hardware-assisted defenses and the increasingly sophisticated attacks that chase them. Protection-key isolation went mainstream through "ERIM: Secure, Efficient In-process Isolation with Protection Keys (MPK)" (USENIX 2019), "Donky" (USENIX 2020), and "xMP: Selective Memory Protection for Kernel and User Space" (S&P 2020), while trusted execution environments drew their own attack surface in "TeeRex: Discovery and Exploitation of Memory Corruption Vulnerabilities in SGX Enclaves" (USENIX 2020) and "A Tale of Two Worlds: Assessing the Vulnerability of Enclave Shielding Runtimes" (CCS 2019). Rowhammer kept defeating each generation of mitigation, with "SMASH" (USENIX 2021), "Half-Double" (USENIX 2022), and especially "BLACKSMITH: Scalable Rowhammering in the Frequency Domain" (S&P 2022) breaking the in-DRAM TRR defenses vendors had shipped; "RETBLEED" (USENIX 2022) did the same on the speculative side. Meanwhile a quieter thread argued for prevention by construction, as memory-safe languages entered the picture through "Towards Memory Safe Enclave Programming with Rust-SGX" (CCS 2019) and "MirChecker: Detecting Bugs in Rust Programs via Static Analysis" (CCS 2021).

The most recent work, clustered in NDSS 2026, shows a field that has absorbed a decade of mitigations and is now probing their seams. With kernel CFI widely deployed, "DirtyFree: Simplified Data-Oriented Programming in the Linux Kernel" revives data-oriented programming as the practical bypass, echoing the 2018 BOP insight, while "PhantomMap: GPU-Assisted Kernel Exploitation" and "Cross-Cache Attacks for the Linux Kernel via PCP Massaging" extend kernel exploitation to new hardware and allocator paths. Bug-class-specific defenses continue to sharpen in "Fast Pointer Nullification for Use-After-Free Prevention" and "IsolatOS: Detecting Double Fetch Bugs in COTS RTOS by Re-enabling Kernel Isolation," and Rowhammer research has turned toward measurement and principled defense in "FLIPPYRAM: A Large-Scale Study of Rowhammer Prevalence" and "Memory Band-Aid: A Principled Rowhammer Defense-in-Depth." Two SoK-style efforts capture the current mood: "SoK: Take a Deep Step into Linux Kernel Hardening Effectiveness from the Offensive-Defensive Perspective" weighs which hardening actually holds up, and "What Do They Fix? LLM-Aided Categorization of Security Patches for Critical Memory Bugs" signals that even the analysis of memory bugs is now being handed to machine learning.
